title: Shift in equilibrium: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ and Cl⁻
objective: Observe the pink colour of the hexaaquacobalt(II) ion and the blue colour of the tetrachlorocobaltate(II) ion
Predict and observe the effect of adding concentrated HCl (a source of Cl-) on the colour
Predict and observe the effect of adding water on the colour
Explain both observations using Le Chatelier's principle, including the role of water as a reactant in the reverse direction

theory.statement: In aqueous solution, cobalt(II) exists in equilibrium between the pink, octahedral hexaaqua ion and the blue, tetrahedral tetrachloro ion: [Co(H2O)6]2+(pink) + 4Cl-(aq) ⇌ [CoCl4]2-(blue) + 6H2O(l). Because the two forms are such visually distinct colours, this is one of the clearest classroom demonstrations of Le Chatelier's principle.
theory.derivationNote: Adding concentrated HCl raises [Cl-] sharply, shifting the equilibrium to the right (towards blue), by Le Chatelier's principle. Adding water has TWO reinforcing effects: it dilutes [Cl-] (shifting left) AND it is itself a product of the reverse reaction being effectively added in large excess (also favouring the reactant side, since water is the solvent and its 'concentration' effectively can't be driven down) — so dilution with water always drives the equilibrium back towards pink, unlike a simple dilution of a solute-only equilibrium.
keyEquations: Adding Cl- (via HCl or NaCl) shifts right (blue); adding water shifts left (pink)

apparatus.name: Concentrated hydrochloric acid
apparatus.why: Provides a large, controllable increase in chloride ion concentration

apparatus.name: Distilled water
apparatus.why: Dilutes the mixture and shifts the equilibrium back

apparatus.name: Water bath (optional)
apparatus.why: Warming also favours the blue form, since the forward reaction is endothermic — useful for cross-checking

procedure.text: Dissolve a little cobalt(II) chloride in the minimum of water to give a pink solution.
Add concentrated HCl drop by drop, noting the colour after each addition.
Once the solution is distinctly blue, add water drop by drop and watch it return towards pink.
Repeat the chloride addition using solid NaCl instead of HCl, for comparison.
Explain both directions of the colour change in terms of Le Chatelier's principle.

steps: Add each reagent to a portion of the cobalt solution
Observe and record the colour (pink / blue / intermediate)
State whether the equilibrium shifted towards products or reactants

expectedResult.quantity: Direction of the equilibrium shift on adding concentrated HCl vs. water
expectedResult.statement: Adding concentrated HCl turns the pink cobalt(II) solution blue (equilibrium shifts towards [CoCl4]2-). Adding water reverses this, turning it pink again (equilibrium shifts back towards [Co(H2O)6]2+) — a clean, reversible demonstration of Le Chatelier's principle running in both directions.

safety: Concentrated HCl is corrosive — use in a fume cupboard or well-ventilated area, wear eye protection.
Cobalt salts are toxic and a suspected carcinogen with prolonged exposure — avoid skin contact and wash hands after.
sourcesOfError: Too little HCl gives only a faint colour change that is hard to judge
The colour change is gradual (not instantaneous), so waiting after each addition matters
Ambient lighting affects how the pink/blue/violet intermediate shades are judged

viva.question: Write the equilibrium and identify which species is pink and which is blue.
viva.expectedConcept: [Co(H2O)6]2+ (pink) + 4Cl- ⇌ [CoCl4]2- (blue) + 6H2O. The hexaaqua ion is pink; the tetrachloro ion is blue.
viva.answerLogic: Correct equation with colours assigned to the correct species.
viva.commonMisconception: Reversing which complex is which colour.

viva.question: Why does adding water shift the equilibrium back to pink, rather than just diluting both colours equally?
viva.expectedConcept: Water is not a spectator here — it is a product of the forward reaction (as written) and its effective concentration cannot be depleted, so adding a large excess of it drives the equilibrium towards the side that consumes it, i.e. back towards [Co(H2O)6]2+.
viva.answerLogic: Water is a reactant in the reverse direction, not merely a diluent.
viva.commonMisconception: Treating water addition as simple dilution with no chemical role.

viva.question: How would raising the temperature affect this equilibrium, and why?
viva.expectedConcept: The forward (pink to blue) reaction is endothermic, so raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium further towards the blue [CoCl4]2- form, by Le Chatelier's principle applied to a temperature stress.
viva.answerLogic: Le Chatelier applied to heat as a 'reagent'.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming temperature has no effect on an ionic equilibrium.

preLab.question: The blue form of the cobalt(II) equilibrium is:
preLab.feedback: The tetrahedral tetrachlorocobaltate(II) ion, [CoCl4]2-, is blue; the hexaaqua ion is pink.

duringLab.question: Observe the colour with at least four different reagents/amounts.

postLab.question: Adding water to the blue solution will:
postLab.feedback: Diluting with water shifts the equilibrium back towards the pink hexaaqua form.

assumptions: Equilibrium is reached quickly relative to observation
HCl and NaCl both act simply as sources of Cl-
edgeCases: Very dilute Cl- keeps the solution pink regardless of small further additions
expectedBehaviour: Pink to blue on adding Cl-; blue to pink on adding water
